items.title: Peace bonds: The colonial tool rearing its head amid protests in 2026
items.summary: In 2023, the Indian parliament enacted three new penal laws: the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), in place of its colonial era ancestors, a move that Union Home Minister Amit Shah said would make the criminal justice system "completely Swadeshi" . Back then, lawyers criticised the "new" statues as "old wine in a new bottle", largely retaining many problematic provisions introduced in colonial times. In 2026, the means adopted by the British Raj of quelling dissent still remain firmly cemented in Indian penal procedures. The recent nationwide protests and the police response to them put these provisions under the spotlight, especially those that deal with preventive policing. Detained protestors were made to sign bonds promising not to cause "breach of peace" for varying amounts of time. Here, we give historical context to these peace bonds, show how they have been retained in current jurisprudence and speak to leading criminal law practitioners on the issue. Medieval England and the colonial roots of peace bonds Over 600 years before the "swadeshi" laws were introduced, on the Sunday before the Feast of the Conversion of St Paul in 1361, King Edward III enacted the Justices of the Peace Act . This 14th-century legislation gave Justices of the Peace - the modern-day equivalents of magistrates - the statutory power to take sureties from people suspected of being threats to peace or of bad character, to secure their good behaviour. This statutory power of "binding over" was generally preventive in nature, not punitive. A few centuries later, with profound political and religious changes, the Justices became lynchpins of monarchs who, in turn, were able to advcance their policing power. Under Queen Elizabeth I , Justices of the Peace were given authority to enquire into all cases of persons accused of maintaining, defending, or extolling - by word or deed - the authority of the Pope in England. As time went by, every monarch and government used the Justices for two main tasks - the enforcement of the new order and the repression of dissent. Whenever political danger was apprehended, a more rigorous execution of the law could easily be brought about by issuing orders to the Justices. items.title: Telangana man alleges police assault, cops file FIRs against him
items.summary: Twenty-two-year-old Mohammed Fayaz was walking home on the night of October 2, just past midnight, on the streets of Mahabubnagar in Telangana. When he was a few hundred metres away from his home in Habibnagar, two police constables on patrol duty, Balaram and Kowdi Raju, allegedly beat him up so badly that he started bleeding from the head. The government hospital that treated Fayaz recorded a laceration on the left side of the head, abrasion on the face, and blunt trauma to the chest, neck and leg. But according to the Mahabubnagar I Town police, the injuries are Fayaz’s own fault. When trying to run away from the constables, they say Fayaz “ran into a nearby house, fell down and sustained a bleeding injury to his head.” While there has been no inquiry or action against the constables so far, the police have booked Fayaz for trespassing into Mohammed Kadar’s house in Habibnagar and intimidating him. Except Kadar, who is named as the complainant, told TNM that this never happened and that he was forced by the I Town police to sign the complaint letter. A YouTuber named Azhar Khan, who reported on the incident and protests against the police by Fayaz and his family, was also booked for defamation of one of the constables. Azhar and Fayaz have insisted that both the cases are false. Fayaz and his family have approached the Telangana High Court to quash both the FIRs against them. They have also demanded a departmental enquiry against the two constables who allegedly assaulted Fayaz. The night of the alleged assault Fayaz, who does upholstery work on autos, is the sole breadwinner in his family. On the night of October 2, he was walking back home around 12.30 am from a dinner hosted by a relative on the occasion of the Gyarvi Sharif festival, according to his lawyer, Mounis Abidi. Fayaz alleges that the two constables, Raju and Balaram, targeted him unprovoked and launched a brutal physical assault. Fayaz has said that as soon as he saw the constables, he instinctively tried to flee, but they allegedly dragged him and rammed his head against a wall, shoved a cycle onto him and hit him on his legs with lathis. Mahabubnagar I Town Station House Officer (SHO) M Appaiah denied these allegations. items.title: Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar vows action against IT companies discriminating against locals
items.summary: Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar on Sunday, October 25 vowed action against IT companies that discriminate against Kannadigas in hirings. While the CM did not specify what kind of action would be taken, he said that his government would not allow the “rights, dignity and opportunities of Kannadigas” to be disregarded for any reason. In a social media post, the Chief Minister said: “It is disheartening to hear complaints that Kannadigas are being denied job opportunities in Bengaluru’s IT companies. The government has taken the issue of native Kannada speakers being sidelined seriously. items.title: How a biodiversity register at CBD COP17 is reclaiming erased Kerala fisher knowledge
items.summary: Nearly a decade after he helped the Kerala State Biodiversity Board (KSBB) document marine life off the Thiruvananthapuram’s coast, marine researcher Robert Panippilla arrived at the UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan with a digital community biodiversity register that is intended to correct a decade-long injustice. The conference, being held from October 19 to 30, 2026, is the first global review of collective progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. “The digital register is a response to the erasure of community knowledge from the marine biodiversity register published by the KSBB in 2017,” Panipilla said, while speaking to TNM at Yerevan in Armenia. According to him, indigenous knowledge was left out of the state’s documentation because scientific experts had failed to identify marine fauna documented by them. Between 2013 and 2015, local fishers led by Robert Panipilla had documented marine biodiversity and the traditional knowledge of local fishing communities in Thiruvananthapuram as part of a KSBB initiative. They documented more than 2,000 species and traditional information provided by 69 knowledge holders. However, when the team submitted its findings, the board appointed five marine scientists to identify and classify the organisms, Panipilla said. He said the scientists could establish the scientific names of only around 500 organisms. “But the KSBB took a highly irresponsible decision. They excluded all organisms the scientists could not identify from the Marine Biodiversity Register,” he alleged. “Normally, all biodiversity-related work should be inclusive. What they did was contrary to that principle.” Developed by Friends of Marine Life (FML), the register was presented by Panipilla at the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17). Professional diver Jestin Jos, who contributed to species identification, also attended the event. The Community Marine Biodiversity Online Register, available at Combor.org , scientifically documents marine species and underwater ecosystems alongside the knowledge of people whose lives and livelihoods are closely tied to the sea.
